```formula
a × f(n / b) ≤ q × f(n),  q < 1
T(n) = Θ(f(n))
where
f(n): the work outside the recursive calls
f(n / b): the work outside the calls in one child call
a: the number of subproblems
b: the shrink factor
n: the input size (the regularity inequality must hold for all large n)
c: the critical exponent, log_b(a)
ε: epsilon, some fixed positive number
q: some fixed constant below 1 (written k in some textbooks)
Ω: Big-Omega, at least a constant times
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
T(n): the running time on input size n
≤: less than or equal to
In words: if the root's work beats the leaf count by a fixed power of n, and the children together always do a fixed fraction less work than their parent, the root's own work dominates.
```

The regularity condition says that the work really does shrink from one level to the next. It holds automatically for ordinary polynomial f, such as f(n) = n^2 with a = 2, b = 2 (two children do 2 × (n/2)^2 = n^2 / 2, half the parent's work); it exists to rule out pathological, wildly oscillating functions.

### The simple version

Most recurrences you'll meet have f(n) = Θ(n^d), a plain power of n. Then just compare d with log_b(a):

```formula
T(n) = a × T(n / b) + Θ(n^d)
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
a: the number of subproblems
b: the shrink factor; each subproblem has size n / b
d: the power of n in the outside work, a constant of at least 0 (d = 1 for a linear merge)
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: the special case where the work outside the calls is a simple power of n, which covers almost every textbook recurrence.
```

| Compare | Result |
|---|---|
| d < log_b a | Θ(n^(log_b a)) |
| d = log_b a | Θ(n^d log n) |
| d > log_b a | Θ(n^d) |

Equivalently, compare a with b^d: the ratio a / b^d is exactly how fast the work per level grows. Above 1, the leaves win; equal to 1, every level ties; below 1, the root wins.

### Worked examples

In the table, the first column is the right-hand side of T(n) = …, and log_b a is the critical exponent:

| Recurrence | a, b | log_b a | f | Case | T(n) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T(n/2) + 1 | 1, 2 | 0 | 1 | 2 | log n |
| 2T(n/2) + n | 2, 2 | 1 | n | 2 | n log n |
| 3T(n/2) + n | 3, 2 | 1.585 | n | 1 | n^1.585 |
| 7T(n/2) + n^2 | 7, 2 | 2.807 | n^2 | 1 | n^2.807 |
| 4T(n/2) + n^2 | 4, 2 | 2 | n^2 | 2 | n^2 log n |
| 2T(n/2) + n^2 | 2, 2 | 1 | n^2 | 3 | n^2 |
| T(n/2) + n | 1, 2 | 0 | n | 3 | n |
| 2T(n/2) + n log n | 2, 2 | 1 | n log n | 2, k=1 | n log^2 n |

## Key takeaways
- Polynomially larger outside work dominates only when the regularity condition also holds.
- For ordinary polynomial outside work, comparing exponents gives the familiar three-case shortcut.
- The worked table applies the same conditions to several common recurrences.

## Further reading
- [Master theorem — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_theorem_(analysis_of_algorithms))
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

lessons.title: When the Master Theorem does not fit
lessons.summary: Recognise unsupported recurrences and prove a guessed bound by induction.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size. First check a theorem’s assumptions; when they fail, a recursion tree and an explicit induction can provide a different route.

## Where the Master Theorem doesn't apply

**Subtract-and-conquer.** Recurrences where the input shrinks by subtracting rather than dividing aren't of the form a × T(n/b). Unroll them instead:

```formula
T(n) = T(n − 1) + n
T(n) = n + (n − 1) + … + 1
T(n) = n × (n + 1) / 2 = Θ(n^2)
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
n: the input size, which drops by 1 per call
…: "and so on" down to 1
Θ(n^2): Big-Theta of n squared, growing like n × n
In words: each call does work equal to its size and passes on a problem only one smaller, so the work adds up to about half of n squared.
```

Likewise T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 doubles at every level for n levels:

```formula
T(n) = 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^{n−1}
T(n) = 2^n − 1 = Θ(2^n)
where
T(n): the number of steps (for Towers of Hanoi, the number of disc moves)
n: the input size (the number of discs)
2^{n−1}: n − 1 copies of 2 multiplied together, the number of calls on the deepest level
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
…: "and so on", doubling each time
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: two calls each one size smaller makes the call count double on every one of n levels.
```

For 10 discs that is 1,023 moves; for 64 discs, about 1.8 × 10^19.

**The gap between cases.** T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n / log n has log_b(a) = log_2(2) = 1, so compare f(n) = n / log n with n^1 = n:

```formula
f(n) = n / log(n)
f(n) / n^{1 − ε} = n^ε / log(n) → ∞
f(n) / n = 1 / log(n) → 0
where
f(n): the work outside the recursive calls
n: the input size
log(n): the logarithm of n
ε: epsilon, any fixed positive number
n^ε: n to the power ε, which outgrows log(n) for any ε > 0
→: "tends to", as n grows
∞: infinity, growing without limit
In words: n over log n is bigger than any n^(1 − ε), so case 1 fails, but smaller than n by a log factor, so case 2 (with k ≥ 0) fails too.
```

So it falls between case 1 and case 2 of the standard statement. (The answer is Θ(n log log n), as the later Akra–Bazzi examples show. Some textbooks state an extended case 2 that allows negative k and covers this directly.)

**Uneven splits.** T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n has two subproblems of different sizes. The Master Theorem needs every subproblem to be n/b.

**Non-constant a or b.** T(n) = √n × T(√n) + n (√n is the square root of n) needs other techniques, such as a change of variables: substitute n = 2^m, so that √n = 2^(m/2) and the recurrence becomes one in m.

## Substitution: guess and prove

When no theorem fits, guess the answer (from a recursion tree) and prove it by **mathematical induction**: assume the bound holds for smaller inputs and show it then holds for n. For merge sort, prove T(n) ≤ c × n × log_2(n) for powers of two n ≥ 2, choosing c large enough to cover T(2). Treat T(1) separately, since log_2(1) = 0:

```formula
T(n) = 2 × T(n/2) + n
T(n) ≤ 2 × c × (n/2) × log_2(n/2) + n
T(n) ≤ c × n × (log_2(n) − 1) + n
T(n) ≤ c × n × log_2(n) − c × n + n
T(n) ≤ c × n × log_2(n)   when c ≥ 1
where
T(n): merge sort's running time on n items
n: the input size, a power of 2 of at least 2
c: the constant in the guessed bound, chosen once and kept fixed
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(n/2) = log_2(n) − 1
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: assuming the bound for half-size inputs, the bound for size n follows with the same c, as long as c is at least 1.
```

The second line uses the assumption for n/2; the last line drops − c × n + n, which is at most 0 when c is at least 1.

> [!warning] The classic induction bug
> "Guess T(n) = O(n). Then T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n ≤ 2c(n/2) + n = cn + n = O(n)." This is wrong. You must prove the *exact* form T(n) ≤ c × n with the same constant c, and c × n + n is not ≤ c × n. Hiding constants inside O during an induction lets you "prove" anything.

## Key takeaways
- Subtracting from input size, uneven splits and some gap functions need other techniques.
- A substitution proof must preserve the same chosen constant through the induction.
- A loose asymptotic simplification inside the proof does not establish the required inequality.

## Further reading
- [Master theorem — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_theorem_(analysis_of_algorithms))
- [Akra–Bazzi method — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akra%E2%80%93Bazzi_method)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

options.text: Θ(n log n), by the Master Theorem with a = 1
options.explanation: The Master Theorem needs subproblems of size n/b with b > 1. Here the subproblem is n - 1, which is 'subtract and conquer', not divide and conquer.
Correct. Unrolling gives n + (n − 1) + ... + 1 = n × (n + 1) / 2 = Θ(n^2).
Each level does linear work, not constant, and there are n levels.
There is only one recursive call per level, so nothing doubles. Exponential 2^n comes from T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1.

```formula
n / log(n) ≠ Θ(n × (log n)^k),  k ≥ 0
where

ε: epsilon, any fixed positive number
k: the power of log n allowed in case 2

Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
```

"Polynomially smaller" means smaller by a factor of n^ε (n to some fixed positive power), and log n is not such a factor.

A student 'proves' that `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n` is O(n), where T(n) is the running time on input size n and c is a fixed positive constant:

options.explanation: Correct. 'c × n + n = O(n)' quietly switches to a bigger constant (c + 1). Repeat that at every level of the induction and the 'constant' grows with log n, which is exactly the hidden log factor.

1. Induction must prove the **same** statement it assumed: T(n) ≤ c × n for one fixed c.
2. The step gives T(n) ≤ c × n + n. For this to be ≤ c × n you'd need n ≤ 0. Impossible.
3. Writing "= O(n)" hides the fact that the constant went from c to c + 1.
4. Applied over log_2(n) levels, the constant becomes about c + log_2(n): precisely the n log n the true answer has.

Doing it properly with the guess T(n) ≤ c × n × log_2(n):

```formula
T(n) ≤ 2 × c × (n/2) × log_2(n/2) + n
T(n) ≤ c × n × log_2(n) − c × n + n
T(n) ≤ c × n × log_2(n)   if c ≥ 1
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
n: the input size, a power of 2 of at least 2
c: the fixed constant in the guess, the same on both sides
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(n/2) = log_2(n) − 1
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: assuming the bound for size n/2 gives the same bound, with the same c, for size n.
```

That one closes, with the same c.

For that final induction, start at n = 2 and choose c to cover T(2); T(1) is handled separately because log_2(1) = 0.

lessons.title: Uneven splits and Akra–Bazzi
lessons.summary: Balance unequal subproblems and account for work across their scales.
lessons.body:
## Akra–Bazzi: the general case

The **Akra–Bazzi** method handles recurrences with several subproblem sizes under regularity assumptions: nonnegative g with suitable polynomial growth, bounded positive base cases, and sufficiently small perturbations of the subproblem sizes. The smooth polynomial/logarithmic examples here satisfy these conditions. The recurrence looks like this:

```formula
T(n) = g(n) + Σ_{i=1}^{m} a_i × T(b_i × n)
a_i > 0,  0 < b_i < 1
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
g(n): the work done outside the recursive calls (the Master Theorem's f(n))
Σ_{i=1}^{m}: capital sigma, "sum of": add up the term for every kind of subproblem i from 1 to m
m: the number of different subproblem sizes
a_i: how many subproblems of kind i each call makes, a positive constant
b_i: the fraction of n that each subproblem of kind i gets, between 0 and 1
i: which kind of subproblem
n: the input size
In words: a call does g(n) work and recurses on several groups of subproblems, each group with its own count and its own fraction of the input.
```

1. Find the unique p that balances the subproblems' total weight:

```formula
Σ_{i=1}^{m} a_i × (b_i)^p = 1
where
Σ_{i=1}^{m}: "sum of" over every kind of subproblem i from 1 to m
a_i: the number of subproblems of kind i
b_i: the fraction of the input each one gets
(b_i)^p: b_i raised to the power p
p: the unknown exponent being solved for
m: the number of kinds of subproblem
i: which kind
In words: p is the power at which the subproblems' sizes, weighted by how many there are, add up to exactly 1.
```

2. Then:

```formula
T(n) = Θ(n^p × (1 + I))
I = ∫_1^n g(u) / u^{p+1} du
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
n: the input size
p: the balancing exponent from step 1
I: an integral that measures how much the outside work g adds across all scales
∫_1^n … du: the integral from 1 to n with respect to u: the area under the curve between u = 1 and u = n, a continuous version of summing
g(u): the outside work at input size u
u: a stand-in variable for the input size, running from 1 to n
u^{p+1}: u raised to the power p + 1
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: start from n^p, the cost if the leaves dominated, and multiply by a correction that grows when the outside work is comparable to or bigger than n^p.
```

The intuition: p plays the role of log_b(a). It is the exponent at which the subproblems' total "weight" exactly balances. Then you compare g with n^p, much like the Master Theorem, but the integral handles the in-between cases smoothly. (It also tolerates small perturbations such as floors and ceilings in the subproblem sizes.)

**Example 1: uneven split.** T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n.

```formula
(1/3)^p + (2/3)^p = 1  gives  p = 1
I = ∫_1^n u / u^2 du = ∫_1^n 1/u du = ln(n)
T(n) = Θ(n × (1 + ln(n))) = Θ(n × log n)
where
p: the balancing exponent; at p = 1 the fractions 1/3 and 2/3 add up to exactly 1
I: the Akra–Bazzi integral
∫_1^n … du: the integral from 1 to n with respect to u, the area under the curve
u: a stand-in for the input size, from 1 to n
ln(n): the natural logarithm of n (base e ≈ 2.718)
log: the logarithm in any base; it differs from ln by a constant factor
T(n): the running time
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: the two pieces add up to the whole input, so every level does about n work, and there are about log n levels.
```

The recursion tree agrees: no level does more than n work, the first log_3(n) levels are complete and do exactly n each, and the deepest path (always taking 2/3) has log_{3/2}(n) levels (the logarithm of n to base 1.5). Both counts are Θ(log n).

## Key takeaways
- Akra–Bazzi allows different subproblem fractions under its regularity assumptions.
- The balancing exponent describes the recursive structure.
- The integral adds the contribution of outside work across scales.

## Further reading
- [Akra–Bazzi method — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akra%E2%80%93Bazzi_method)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

questions.prompt: Solve `T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/4) + n`, where T(n) is the running time on input size n (use Akra–Bazzi, or reason about the recursion tree).

options.explanation: This would need each level to do about n work. Here the subproblem sizes add up to only 3/4 of the parent's size, so level totals shrink.
This treats it like 3T(n/2) + n. The two subproblems here are smaller than that (n/2 and n/4, not three of n/2).
Correct. The p that makes (1/2)^p + (1/4)^p = 1 is below 1 (the sum is 3/4 at p = 1). The Akra–Bazzi integral then grows like n^(1−p), so T = Θ(n^p × n^(1−p)) = Θ(n). The root dominates.
The root alone does n work, so T(n) is at least n.

questions.workedExample:
**Recursion tree view.** Each level's total is 3/4 of the level above, because n/2 + n/4 = (3/4) × n:

```formula
W_k = (3/4)^k × n
T(n) ≈ n × (1 + 3/4 + 9/16 + …)
T(n) ≈ n × 1 / (1 − 3/4) = 4 × n
where
W_k: the total work on level k of the recursion tree
k: the level number, 0 at the root
(3/4)^k: k copies of 3/4 multiplied together
T(n): the total running time
n: the input size
…: "and so on"
≈: approximately equal to (the tree is cut off at size 1)
In words: the level totals shrink by a quarter each time, a geometric series that adds up to at most 4 times the root's work.
```

So Θ(n).

**Akra–Bazzi view.**

```formula
(1/2)^p + (1/4)^p = 1
x + x^2 = 1,  x = (1/2)^p ≈ 0.618
p = log_2(1 / 0.618) ≈ 0.69
I ≈ n^{1−p} / (1 − p)
T(n) = Θ(n^p × (1 + I)) = Θ(n)
where
p: the balancing exponent; at p = 1 the sum is only 0.75, so p < 1
x: shorthand for (1/2)^p; then (1/4)^p = x^2, and x is the golden ratio minus 1
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
I: the Akra–Bazzi integral of u / u^(p+1) = u^(−p) from 1 to n
n^{1−p}: n raised to the power 1 − p
T(n): the running time
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the subproblem weights balance at p ≈ 0.69, and the integral restores the missing n^(1 − p), leaving exactly linear time.
```

Same pattern as median of medians: if the subproblem sizes total less than n, linear work at the root wins.

lessons.title: Akra–Bazzi worked examples
lessons.summary: Apply the general method to linear selection and a gap between Master Theorem cases.
lessons.body:
The previous unit introduced the balancing exponent and outside-work integral. Here n is the input size. These examples apply that method to selection and a recurrence whose outside work lies between the standard Master Theorem cases.

## Two applications

**Example 2: median of medians.** The linear-time selection algorithm satisfies T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n.

```formula
(1/5)^1 + (7/10)^1 = 0.9 < 1
(1/5)^p + (7/10)^p = 1  gives  p ≈ 0.84
I ≈ n^{1−p} / (1 − p)
T(n) = Θ(n^p × n^{1−p}) = Θ(n)
where
p: the balancing exponent; since the sum is below 1 at p = 1, p must be smaller than 1
I: the Akra–Bazzi integral, here ∫ of u / u^(p+1) = u^(−p) from 1 to n
n^{1−p}: n raised to the power 1 − p
T(n): the running time of median-of-medians selection on n items
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the two subproblems together are only 90% of the input, so the work per level shrinks geometrically and the root's linear work dominates.
```

**Example 3: the gap case.** T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n / log n. Here p = 1, since 2 × (1/2)^1 = 1:

```formula
I = ∫_2^n 1 / (u × ln(u)) du = ln(ln(n)) + C
T(n) = Θ(n × (1 + ln(ln(n))))
T(n) = Θ(n × log log n)
where
I: the Akra–Bazzi integral with g(u) = u / ln(u) and p = 1
∫_2^n … du: the integral from 2 to n with respect to u, the area under the curve
u: a stand-in for the input size
ln: the natural logarithm (base e ≈ 2.718)
C: a constant from the lower limit, which disappears inside Θ
T(n): the running time
n: the input size
log log n: the logarithm of the logarithm of n, which grows extremely slowly (log_2 log_2 of a billion is about 5)
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: the outside work is just a log factor below n, and summed over all levels that adds only a log-log factor.
```

The integral starts at 2 rather than 1 to avoid dividing by ln(1) = 0; the lower limit only changes constants.

## Key takeaways
- Subproblem fractions whose total is below one can lead to geometrically shrinking outside work.
- The integral distinguishes near-linear gap cases from the ordinary balanced case.
- A fixed lower integration limit avoids singularities without changing the growth class.

## Further reading
- [Akra–Bazzi method — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akra%E2%80%93Bazzi_method)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

questions.prompt:
Which tight growth bound describes this recurrence? Use a bounded positive base case and consider sufficiently large input size n.

```formula
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n / log_2(n)
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
n: the input size, larger than the fixed base-case threshold
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n
In words: two half-size calls are followed by slightly less than linear outside work.
```

options.explanation: The outside contributions still accumulate over the levels; the slowly growing log-log factor cannot be dropped.
This would apply to linear outside work. Dividing that work by a logarithm reduces the accumulated factor.
Correct. The balancing exponent is one, and the outside-work integral grows like the logarithm of a logarithm.
The recurrence has half-size calls and sublinear outside work; there is no quadratic root or leaf contribution.

questions.workedExample:
1. The two half-size subproblems give balancing exponent one.
2. A logarithm-base change rescales outside work by a constant, so natural logarithms are convenient for the integral.

```formula
2 × (1/2)^p = 1
p = 1
I = ∫_2^n 1 / (u ln(u)) du
I = ln(ln(n)) + C
T(n) = Θ(n(1 + ln(ln(n))))
where
p: the balancing exponent
I: the Akra–Bazzi integral, written after ignoring a constant logarithm-base factor
∫_2^n … du: the integral from 2 to n with respect to u
u: the input scale inside the integral
ln: the natural logarithm
C: a fixed constant from the lower integration limit
T(n): the running time on input size n
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, a tight growth bound up to fixed factors
In words: the work accumulated across scales adds a slowly growing log-log factor to the linear leaf cost.
```

3. Starting at two avoids the zero logarithm at one. The fixed lower limit does not change the eventual growth bound.

lessons.title: Estimating a feasible input budget
lessons.summary: Use an explicitly assumed operation rate to screen algorithm choices.
lessons.body:
Asymptotic analysis is a model. It is an excellent one, and for large enough inputs it predicts the winner. But it deliberately throws away information: constant factors, the memory hierarchy, the language runtime, and what your inputs actually look like. Experts know both the model and where it leaks.

This lesson is about using complexity as an engineering tool rather than an exam answer.

## What fits in one second

The most practical skill is estimating from the input size n which complexity you can afford. For the arithmetic exercise below, **assume 10^8 counted operations per second** and unit leading constants. This is a hypothetical model, not measured throughput or a guarantee for any language. The estimate is one division:

```formula
t = W(n) / r
where
t: the estimated running time, in seconds (s)
W(n): the number of operations the algorithm does on input size n, read off its complexity with the constant taken as 1 (for example n^2 for a quadratic algorithm)
n: the input size
r: the assumed speed, 10^8 (a hundred million) operations per second
In words: divide the operation count by the speed; anything that comes out near 1 second or less fits the budget.
```

In the table, n! is n factorial (n × (n − 1) × … × 1), 2^n is n copies of 2 multiplied together, and log n is the base-2 logarithm of n:

| Largest n (about 1 s) | Affordable complexity |
|---|---|
| 10 to 11 | O(n!) |
| 20 to 25 | O(2^n) |
| ~500 | O(n^3) |
| ~5,000 to 10,000 | O(n^2) |
| ~10^6 | O(n log n) |
| ~10^8 | O(n) |
| large n, subject to constants and storage | O(log n), O(1) |

The table comes straight from the arithmetic:

```formula
11! ≈ 4 × 10^7
2^25 ≈ 3.4 × 10^7
500^3 = 1.25 × 10^8
(10^4)^2 = 10^8
10^6 × log_2(10^6) ≈ 2 × 10^7
where
11!: 11 factorial, 11 × 10 × … × 1 = 39,916,800
2^25: 25 copies of 2 multiplied together, 33,554,432
500^3: 500 × 500 × 500
log_2(10^6): the base-2 logarithm of a million, about 19.9
≈: approximately equal to
In words: at each table row's largest n, the operation count comes out at about 10^7 to 10^8, which is about a second or less at 10^8 operations per second.
```

Read it backwards too. If a problem says n is up to 200,000, a quadratic algorithm needs about 200,000 × 200,000 = 4 × 10^10 operations, 400 seconds at the assumed rate (minutes rather than a second), so you need O(n log n) or better. If n is at most 20, exponential brute force over subsets may be the simplest correct answer.

> [!note] Content gap: cross-language timings
> A reproducible benchmark for the claimed universal Python-to-compiled speed ratio is absent, so that ratio is omitted. Interpreter version, operation type, data and hardware matter. Native built-ins or vectorisation can reduce interpreter overhead; measure the actual workload.

## Key takeaways
- An operation budget is useful only with a stated rate and cost model.
- Large quadratic counts can rule out an approach before implementation.
- Small inputs can make exhaustive search a sensible starting point.

## Further reading
- [Time complexity guide — USACO Guide](https://usaco.guide/bronze/time-comp)

questions.prompt: At input size n = 200,000, assume exactly 10^8 counted operations per second and unit leading constants. Which listed operation-count growth fits a one-second budget?

options.explanation: 200,000 squared is 4 × 10^10 operations. At around 10^8 per second, that's about 400 seconds, several minutes, far over budget.
200,000 cubed is 8 × 10^15 operations, which would take years at 10^8 per second.
2 multiplied by itself 200,000 times is a number with about 60,000 digits. Exponential algorithms are only feasible for n around 20 to 25.
Correct. 200,000 × log2(200,000) (the base-2 logarithm, about 17.6) is roughly 3.5 × 10^6 operations: comfortably under a second.

questions.workedExample:
Use the hypothetical assumption of 10^8 simple operations per second, and divide each operation count by it:

```formula
t = W / r
n × log_2(n) ≈ 2 × 10^5 × 17.6
n × log_2(n) ≈ 3.5 × 10^6
t ≈ 3.5 × 10^6 / 10^8 ≈ 0.04 s
n^2 = 4 × 10^10,  t = 400 s
n^3 = 8 × 10^15,  t = 8 × 10^7 s
where
t: the estimated running time, in seconds (s)
W: the operation count for a given complexity at this n
r: the assumed speed, 10^8 operations per second
n: the input size, 200,000 = 2 × 10^5
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n, about 17.6 for 200,000
n^2, n^3: n × n and n × n × n
s: seconds; 8 × 10^7 s is about 2.5 years
≈: approximately equal to
In words: only the n log n count comes in under a second; quadratic takes minutes and cubic takes years.
```

| Complexity | Operations at n = 2 × 10^5 | Time |
|---|---|---|
| n log n | ~3.5 × 10^6 | ~0.04 s |
| n^2 | 4 × 10^10 | ~400 s |
| n^3 | 8 × 10^15 | ~2.5 years |

So O(n log n) is the slowest that fits. (O(n) would also fit, with more room to spare.) Reading constraints this way tells you which kind of algorithm a problem expects.

questions.prompt: You must choose a subset of at most **n = 20** items that satisfies a tricky constraint, and the code runs once a day. What is the most sensible first approach? Assume each subset can be checked in at most 20 cheap operations.

options.text: Brute force is exponential, so it must be avoided; research a polynomial algorithm
options.explanation: Exponential doesn't mean slow at every n. For n = 20 the brute force is fast, and a clever algorithm adds complexity and bug risk for no benefit.

options.text: Try all orderings (20!) to be safe
options.explanation: 20! (20 factorial, 20 × 19 × … × 1) is about 2.4 × 10^18, which would take centuries. Subsets (2 to the power n) and orderings (n factorial) are very different sizes.
Correct. There are 1,048,576 subsets, so the stated check costs at most about 21 million operations. Benchmark whether that fits the daily job budget.

options.text: Use a randomised heuristic, since exact answers are infeasible
options.explanation: Exact answers are entirely feasible at this size, and a heuristic could miss the right subset.

questions.workedExample:
Count the subsets, then multiply by the cost of checking each:

```formula
S = 2^n = 2^20 = 1048576
W ≤ S × n = 1048576 × 20 ≈ 2.1 × 10^7
t ≈ 2.1 × 10^7 / 10^8 ≈ 0.2 s
20! ≈ 2.4 × 10^18
where
S: the number of subsets of n items (each item is either in or out)
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
n: the number of items, here 20
W: the total number of operations, at most 20 per subset
t: the estimated running time at an assumed 10^8 operations per second, in seconds (s)
20!: 20 factorial, the number of orderings of 20 items
s: seconds
≤: less than or equal to
≈: approximately equal to
In words: about a million subsets at 20 steps each is about twenty million operations, a fraction of a second, while trying every ordering would be about 10^11 times more.
```

Actual runtime must be measured for the implementation. The feasibility table says O(2^n) is fine up to about n = 20 to 25, O(n!) only up to about 10 or 11.

questions.prompt: A loop performs 4 × 10^8 iterations. A representative benchmark on the target machine measured between 10^6 and 10^7 iterations per second. What runtime does that measured range predict?

options.text: Around 0.04 s, because computers do billions of operations a second
options.explanation: The measured rate in the question already includes the implementation and hardware costs. CPU clock rate alone does not determine iteration throughput.
Correct. Divide 4 × 10^8 by the stated rates: 40 to 400 seconds, or tens of seconds to several minutes.
Four seconds would require 10^8 iterations/s, above the stated measured range.
The stated range predicts 40–400 seconds, not hours.

questions.workedExample:
Divide the iteration count by each end of the measured rate:

```formula
t = I / r
t_fast = 4 × 10^8 / 10^7 = 40 s
t_slow = 4 × 10^8 / 10^6 = 400 s
where
t: the predicted running time, in seconds (s)
I: the number of loop iterations, 4 × 10^8
r: the measured speed, in iterations per second
t_fast: the time at the fast end of the range, 10^7 iterations per second
t_slow: the time at the slow end, 10^6 iterations per second
s: seconds; 400 s is about 6.7 minutes
In words: four hundred million iterations at one to ten million per second takes forty seconds to under seven minutes.
```

This estimate applies only if the benchmark remains representative at the larger input. The numbers are scenario assumptions, not a universal Python speed claim.

lessons.title: Constants, locality and theoretical winners
lessons.summary: Explain practical performance differences hidden by asymptotic labels.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size unless an example names another dimension. The asymptotic model leaves out factors that must be measured on the actual workload.

## Constant factors

Big-O hides constants, but the computer doesn't. Two algorithms in the same class can differ by 10x, and an asymptotically worse one can win for all inputs you'll ever see.

The standard example is sorting small arrays. Insertion sort is Θ(n^2), but its inner loop is tiny, branch-predictable and works entirely in cache. For small n it beats merge sort and quicksort, so real libraries use **hybrid sorts**:

- **Timsort-style natural merge sorts** extend short runs with binary insertion sort, then merge them. Thresholds differ by implementation; modern CPython uses a Powersort merge policy, so a single threshold/policy should not be attributed to both Python and Java.
- **Introsort** (C++ `std::sort` in common implementations) runs quicksort, switches to heapsort if the recursion gets too deep (guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case), and leaves small partitions (16 elements in libstdc++) for a final insertion sort pass.

The general lesson: the crossover point is found by measurement, not theory.

## The memory hierarchy

The RAM model treats memory accesses uniformly, but real machines have caches, main memory and storage with different access costs.

> [!note] Content gap: hardware latency measurements
> The repository contains no reproducible measurement setup for the original latency table. Exact nanosecond and microsecond figures are omitted; consult the target hardware documentation and benchmark its access patterns. Cache-line size is hardware-specific (64 bytes is common on x86; ARM implementations vary).

So **access patterns** matter enormously:

- **Arrays vs linked lists.** Summing an array and summing a linked list are both Θ(n). But the array is contiguous: a 64-byte cache line holds eight 8-byte values and the prefetcher streams the rest. A linked list's nodes can be scattered across memory, and each `next` pointer must be loaded before the following address is known, so ordinary demand loads form a dependency chain and are harder to overlap. The list is often several times slower, and much worse when nodes are scattered.
- **Traversal order.** C stores 2D arrays row by row. For an N by N array of 8-byte values, both loops below are Θ(N^2), touching all N × N elements once:

```c
/* row order: sequential */
/* j changes fastest: stay in one row. */
for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
        sum += a[i][j];

/* column order: N*8-byte jumps */
/* i changes fastest: visit each row. */
for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
        sum += a[i][j];
```

For large N (so the matrix doesn't fit in cache), the column-order loop touches a new cache line on almost every access and can be several times slower, sometimes by an order of magnitude.

This is why B-trees, with hundreds of keys per node, beat binary search trees for databases and file systems: they need far fewer memory or disk accesses for the same Θ(log n) search. Cache-aware and **cache-oblivious** algorithms are designed around counting cache misses instead of instructions.

## Galactic algorithms

Some algorithms have the best known asymptotic complexity but are never used, because their constants are astronomical. They're nicknamed **galactic algorithms**: they would only win on inputs larger than anything that fits on Earth.

- **Matrix multiplication.** For n by n matrices, the naive algorithm is Θ(n^3) and Strassen's is about Θ(n^2.807). Theoretical algorithms descending from Coppersmith–Winograd have pushed the exponent below 2.372, but they are useless in practice. Even Strassen is used only above a size threshold, if at all; optimised BLAS libraries mostly rely on carefully blocked Θ(n^3) code that uses the cache brilliantly.
- **Integer multiplication.** For n-digit numbers, Harvey and van der Hoeven's 2019 algorithm runs in O(n log n), believed optimal, but only beats existing methods for astronomically large numbers. Practical libraries such as GMP switch between schoolbook, Karatsuba, Toom–Cook variants and FFT-based multiplication at tuned size thresholds.

The opposite trap also exists: assuming a fancy algorithm is needed when the simple one, with a good constant, is fast enough.

## Key takeaways
- Constant factors and memory access patterns can determine measured performance.
- Sequential array traversal has better locality than scattered dependent accesses.
- An asymptotically better algorithm may have constants that make it impractical.

## Further reading
- [Locality of reference — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality_of_reference)
- [Galactic algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galactic_algorithm)
- [Introsort — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introsort)
- [Timsort — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timsort)

questions.prompt: On a target machine with 64-byte cache lines, an array traversal benchmarks faster than traversing a linked list whose nodes are scattered across the heap. Both sum the same n integers in Θ(n) time (time proportional to n). What explains a possible gap?

options.text: The array has contiguous access and spatial locality; the list follows dependent pointers that may miss in cache
options.explanation: Correct. The next node address depends on loading the current node. This serial dependency and poor spatial locality can make scattered traversal slower; exact latency requires target-specific measurement.

options.text: Linked lists are Θ(n log n) to traverse because of pointer overhead
options.explanation: Traversal is still Θ(n), proportional to the number of nodes n: one step per node. The difference is in the constant factor per step, not the growth rate.

options.text: The compiler can't optimise linked list code at all
options.explanation: Compilers optimise both fine. The bottleneck is memory latency, which no compiler can remove from a pointer-chasing loop.

options.text: Linked lists store more data, so there's more to add up
options.explanation: The values added are the same. The extra pointer per node increases memory traffic a bit, but the main cost is latency from scattered, dependent accesses.

questions.workedExample:
1. With 4-byte integers and 64-byte lines, a line can contain 64 / 4 = 16 adjacent array values.
2. A scattered list may need a new line for each node, and its next address depends on the current load.
3. These access patterns can have different costs despite the same Θ(n) count.

Content gap: no reproducible hardware measurements support a universal cache-miss latency or speed ratio, so those numeric claims are omitted.

link.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know

options.text: B, because it accesses columns, which are stored contiguously in C
options.explanation: C stores arrays row by row, not column by column. Fortran, MATLAB and Julia are column-major, but C is row-major.

options.text: Neither: both are Θ(N^2) and do the same additions
options.explanation: They have the same complexity, Θ(N^2) (N × N additions), and the same arithmetic, but very different memory access patterns. Big-O doesn't capture that.

options.text: A walks sequentially; B advances by 80,000 bytes in its inner loop
options.explanation: Correct. In A, consecutive accesses are 8 bytes apart, so each cache line serves 8 doubles and the prefetcher helps. In B, consecutive accesses are a full row (10,000 × 8 bytes) apart.

options.text: A, because it has fewer loop iterations
options.explanation: Both do exactly 10,000 × 10,000 = 10^8 iterations. The difference is entirely in the cost per memory access.

questions.workedExample:
Work out where each element lives in memory:

```formula
addr(i, j) = (i × N + j) × 8 B
step_A = 8 B
step_B = N × 8 B = 80000 B
size = N × N × 8 B = 8 × 10^8 B = 800 MB
where
addr(i, j): the byte offset of a[i][j] from the start of the array
i: the row index
j: the column index
N: the number of rows and of columns, 10,000
step_A: the distance between consecutive accesses in loop A (j changes fastest)
step_B: the distance between consecutive accesses in loop B (i changes fastest)
size: the total size of the array
B: bytes; each double is 8 bytes
MB: megabytes; 1 MB = 10^6 bytes
In words: in row-major order neighbours in a row are 8 bytes apart, but neighbours in a column are a whole row, 80,000 bytes, apart.
```

1. Loop A: one 64-byte cache line serves 64 / 8 = 8 accesses.
2. Loop B: a different cache line every time.
3. Whether B retains lines for the next column depends on cache capacity, associativity and the column working set; exceeding total cache capacity alone does not prove eviction.

Result: A has better spatial locality; measure the actual speed difference. Same Θ(N^2), very different constants.

questions.prompt: Consider a natural merge sort on n items that uses binary insertion sort to extend short runs to a bounded target of at most 64 elements. Why can this quadratic subroutine fit an O(n log n) overall sort?

options.text: Because insertion sort is Θ(n) on every input
options.explanation: Insertion sort is Θ(n) only on already-sorted (or nearly sorted) input, and Θ(n^2), growing like n × n, in the worst case.

options.text: Because insertion sort uses less memory than merge sort for large n
options.explanation: It's true insertion sort is in place, but that's not why it's used here. It's chosen for speed on small pieces.

options.text: To guarantee stability, which merge sort can't provide
options.explanation: Merge sort is stable, and so is Timsort's merge step. Stability isn't the reason.

options.text: For small n, insertion sort's low constant factors and cache-friendly access make it faster than merging, and the run length is bounded so the quadratic cost is capped
options.explanation: Correct. With runs capped at 64 elements, each insertion sort costs at most about 64 × 64 / 2 steps, a constant. Across n / 64 runs that is O(n) in total, and it beats recursive merging on tiny arrays.

questions.workedExample:
1. Asymptotic class matters for large n. For n around 32 to 64, constants dominate.
2. Insertion sort's inner loop is a few instructions, works on data already in cache, and is very fast on nearly-sorted data (which Timsort exploits).
3. The quadratic part is bounded:

```formula
W_ins ≤ (n / m) × m^2 = n × m
W_ins ≤ n × 64 = O(n)
where
W_ins: the total work of all the insertion sorts
n: the number of items being sorted
m: the maximum run length, here 64
m^2: m × m, the worst-case cost of insertion-sorting one run
O(n): at most a constant times n
≤: less than or equal to
In words: about n / m runs, each costing at most m squared, add up to m times n, which is linear because m is a fixed 64.
```

4. The merges then cost O(n log n) overall, which dominates.

Introsort does the same with a threshold of 16 elements in libstdc++. The crossover is found by benchmarking.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes replacing your BLAS matrix multiply (blocked Θ(n^3), proportional to n × n × n for n by n matrices) with an implementation of a recent algorithm with exponent about 2.37, for multiplying 10,000 x 10,000 matrices. What is the best response?

options.text: Keep the existing baseline until representative benchmarks show that the proposed implementation is faster and meets memory and accuracy needs
options.explanation: Correct. A smaller asymptotic exponent alone does not establish performance at n = 10,000. Constants, implementation, memory and numerical behaviour matter.

options.text: Adopt it: n^2.37 is about 300 times less work than n^3 at n = 10,000
options.explanation: The exponent comparison (10,000 to the power 3 − 2.37 = 0.63 is about 330) ignores the constants, which for these algorithms are so enormous that they only win for matrices far larger than any computer can store.

options.text: Adopt it only for square matrices, since the exponent only applies to them
options.explanation: Squareness isn't the issue. The issue is enormous hidden constants and complexity.

options.text: Use Strassen's algorithm instead, since it is always faster than Θ(n^3)
options.explanation: Strassen has a lower exponent but higher constants, extra memory and worse numerical stability. Whether it helps depends on size and hardware, and it is often not used at all in tuned libraries.

questions.workedExample:
1. An exponent-only ratio ignores leading constants and lower-order work.
2. Require a concrete implementation and benchmark representative shapes, sizes and numeric types.
3. Check accuracy and peak memory as well as time.
4. Keep the measured baseline until the alternative demonstrates an improvement.

questions.prompt: Which factors can explain why a Θ(n²) algorithm beats a Θ(n log n) algorithm over a particular finite input range? Here n is the input size, n² is n × n and log n is its base-2 logarithm. Select all that apply. Let A be Θ(n log n) and B be Θ(n²).

options.text: Inputs are always tiny, say n <= 30
options.explanation: Yes. Below the crossover point the asymptotic class doesn't decide anything; a simple quadratic loop with tiny constants often wins. This is why sorting libraries use insertion sort for small pieces.

options.text: A chases pointers through scattered heap nodes, while B scans a contiguous array
options.explanation: Yes. Dependent cache misses can inflate A’s measured cost per operation. Exact latency depends on hardware and workload.

options.text: A's constant factor is hundreds of times larger than B's
options.explanation: Yes. If A takes 500 × n × log2 n steps and B takes n × n, B is faster for all n up to several thousand. Whether that matters depends on your real n.

options.text: Larger n alone guarantees that the quadratic algorithm wins
options.explanation: False. Growth favours n log n eventually, but no specific finite crossover follows without constants.

options.text: Both are written in the same programming language
options.explanation: No. Using the same language puts them on equal footing; it doesn't favour B. (A slower language for A would only add a constant factor.)

questions.workedExample:
B can win only while its lower constant outweighs its worse growth:

1. **Small n.** Below the crossover, B wins.
2. **Memory behaviour.** Cache misses inflate A's effective constant.
3. **Big constant.** Find where the two costs are equal:

```formula
c_A × n × log_2(n) = c_B × n^2
n / log_2(n) = c_A / c_B
500 × n × log_2(n) = n^2
n = 500 × log_2(n),  n ≈ 6310
where
c_A: A's constant factor, here 500
c_B: B's constant factor, here 1
n: the input size
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n (log_2(6310) ≈ 12.6)
n^2: n squared, n × n
≈: approximately equal to
In words: dividing both sides by n shows the crossover is where n over its own log equals the ratio of the constants; with a 500-to-1 ratio that happens at about n = 6,310.
```

| n | 500 n log2 n | n^2 |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 5.0 × 10^6 | 1.0 × 10^6 |
| 5,000 | 3.1 × 10^7 | 2.5 × 10^7 |
| 6,000 | 3.8 × 10^7 | 3.6 × 10^7 |
| 8,000 | 5.2 × 10^7 | 6.4 × 10^7 |

4. **Larger n alone:** does not favour B; eventual asymptotic superiority does not specify a finite crossover.
5. **Same language:** neutral.

The practical rule: know your real n, then measure.

lessons.title: Hostile inputs and worst-case bounds
lessons.summary: Recognise when an attacker can force expensive algorithm paths.
lessons.body:
Here n counts input items or characters, as stated in each example. Hostile input makes worst-case behaviour an engineering concern.

## Worst case and adversaries

Average-case performance is fine when inputs are benign. When an attacker controls the input, they will find your worst case.

- **Hash flooding.** Hash tables give O(1) average lookups, but if many keys collide, operations degrade to O(n) for a table of n keys, and inserting n colliding keys becomes Θ(n^2): about n × n / 2 comparisons. In 2011, researchers showed that many web frameworks could be knocked over by a single POST request whose parameter names all collided. Languages responded by randomising their hash functions per process. Python has randomised `str` hashing by default since 3.3 and uses SipHash since 3.4.
- **Regular expression backtracking.** Many regex engines use backtracking, which is exponential on some patterns and inputs. In July 2019 a single badly behaved regular expression exhausted CPU across Cloudflare's network and caused a global outage. RE2 and Rust's `regex` provide bounded search complexity for supported patterns. Rust documents O(mn) for individual searches (pattern size m, haystack size n), while repeated-match iterators can reach O(mn²). A fixed-pattern single search is linear in n.
- **Quicksort on sorted input.** A first- or last-element pivot can turn sorted distinct input into Θ(n²). Randomisation gives an expected bound; introsort's heapsort fallback provides the worst-case bound.

If an input could be hostile, choose algorithms with good **worst-case** bounds, or randomise.

## Key takeaways
- User-controlled input can expose an algorithm’s worst paths.
- Hash collisions, regex backtracking and bad pivots can amplify work.
- Choose a suitable worst-case guarantee or stated randomisation model for the workload.

## Further reading
- [Introsort — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introsort)

questions.prompt: In which of these situations should you design for the **worst case** because the input could be adversarial? Select all that apply.

options.text: A public web API stores request parameters in a hash table keyed by attacker-supplied strings
options.explanation: Yes. With a predictable hash function, an attacker can send keys that all collide, making each insert O(n) for a table of n keys and n inserts Θ(n^2), about n × n / 2 steps: the 2011 hash flooding attacks. Randomised (keyed) hashing defends against it.

options.text: A web application firewall runs a backtracking regular expression over every incoming request
options.explanation: Yes. Backtracking can be superlinear or exponential depending on the pattern. Cloudflare's July 2019 incident involved a quadratic regex, not an exponential one.

options.text: A script sorts a fixed list of 12 configuration entries at start-up
options.explanation: No. The input is tiny and fully controlled by you. Even a quadratic sort is instant.

options.text: A service sorts user-uploaded files with a quicksort that always picks the first element as pivot
options.explanation: Yes. Already-sorted uploads (common, and easy for an attacker to craft) trigger the Θ(n^2) case, about n × n / 2 comparisons for n items. Use random pivots or a library sort with guaranteed O(n log n).

options.text: An internal batch job sums the values in a list
options.explanation: No. Summing is Θ(n) on every input; there is no slower worst case for anyone to trigger.

questions.workedExample:
Ask two questions: can someone outside your control choose the input, and does the algorithm have a much worse worst case than its typical case? Here n is the size of the input.

| Situation | Hostile input? | Bad worst case? |
|---|---|---|
| Hash on user keys | yes | O(n) per op |
| Regex on requests | yes | superlinear, up to exponential |
| Sort 12 configs | no | irrelevant |
| Naive quicksort on uploads | yes | Θ(n^2) |
| Sum a list | - | none |

When both answers are yes, you need worst-case guarantees or randomisation.

lessons.title: Measuring and choosing an algorithm
lessons.summary: Use doubling ratios and realistic constraints to choose a suitable implementation.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size. Measurement complements operation counting by exposing hidden costs and practical crossover points.

## Measuring: the doubling experiment

You can estimate the exponent of an algorithm empirically. Time it at n, 2n, 4n and look at the ratios. These numbers are illustrative, not recorded measurements:

| n | time | ratio |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 0.05 s | |
| 2,000 | 0.20 s | 4.0 |
| 4,000 | 0.81 s | 4.05 |
| 8,000 | 3.30 s | 4.07 |

Why does the ratio reveal the exponent? If the running time is roughly a power of n, doubling n multiplies it by 2 to that power, and the constant cancels:

```formula
T(n) ≈ c × n^k
T(2 × n) / T(n) ≈ (2 × n)^k / n^k = 2^k
k ≈ log_2(ratio)
k ≈ log_2(4.07) ≈ 2.02
where
T(n): the measured running time at input size n, in seconds (s)
c: an unknown constant (machine speed, language, implementation), which cancels in the ratio
n: the input size
k: the exponent being estimated
2^k: k copies of 2 multiplied together
ratio: the measured T(2n) / T(n)
log_2: the base-2 logarithm: log_2(x) is the power you raise 2 to in order to get x
≈: approximately equal to
In words: if doubling the input roughly quadruples the time, the time grows like n squared.
```

A ratio of 4 means k = 2: quadratic. A ratio of 2 means linear; slightly above 2 suggests n log n; 8 means cubic. The method assumes the time is close to a single power of n over the range measured; constant start-up costs or a change in cache behaviour between sizes can distort the ratios. This catches the "it's O(n) on paper but quadratic in practice" bugs from hidden costs (the code-analysis lessons).

Measure carefully: warm up first (JIT compilers, caches), repeat runs and take the minimum or median, and use realistic data. In Python, the `timeit` module handles the repetition for you, and a profiler (such as `cProfile`) tells you where the time actually goes.

## Choosing between algorithms

A practical checklist:

1. **How big is n, really?** Today and in a few years. If n will never exceed 1,000, an O(n^2) algorithm doing 1,000 × 1,000 = a million cheap steps is probably fine.
2. **Typical or worst case?** Is the input adversarial or user-controlled? Do you have latency requirements (tail latency) or just throughput?
3. **Memory.** Will the faster algorithm's extra space fit? (The space-complexity lessons.)
4. **Constants and hardware.** Contiguous arrays and sequential access are fast; pointer chasing is slow.
5. **Simplicity.** Simpler code has fewer bugs and is easier to change. Use the simplest algorithm that is fast enough for the largest n you expect.
6. **Use the library.** Standard library sorts, hash maps and heaps are heavily tuned. Beating them is rarely worth the effort.
7. **Measure.** Knuth's line, "premature optimization is the root of all evil", continues: "yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%". Profile to find that 3%.

> [!example] A realistic decision
> You need the top 10 scores from n = 50 million records. Sorting is O(n log n). A size-10 heap scan is O(n log 10), effectively O(n), and uses tiny memory. Quickselect is O(n) average. At n = 5 × 10^7, the heap scan is simple, streaming (no need to hold all records) and fast, making it a suitable starting point to benchmark, even though sorting would also "work".

## Key takeaways
- Doubling experiments suggest growth only over the range and conditions measured.
- Profile realistic data to find which operations dominate.
- Choose the simplest approach that meets the input, memory and latency constraints.

## Further reading
- [timeit — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/timeit.html)

questions.prompt: You time a function at input sizes n = 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 and get 0.1 s, 0.8 s and 6.4 s. What complexity does this suggest?

options.explanation: Linear would double the time when n doubles. Here it goes up 8-fold.
Correct. Each doubling of n multiplies the time by 8 = 2^3 (2 × 2 × 2), so the exponent is 3.
Quadratic would give a ratio of 4 per doubling (0.1, 0.4, 1.6). The measured ratio is 8.
Exponential growth would explode far faster: going from n = 1,000 to 2,000 would multiply the time by 2 to the power 1,000, not 8.

questions.workedExample:
Take the ratios, then turn the ratio into an exponent:

```formula
0.8 s / 0.1 s = 8
6.4 s / 0.8 s = 8
T(n) ≈ c × n^k
T(2 × n) / T(n) ≈ 2^k = 8
k = log_2(8) = 3
where
T(n): the measured running time at input size n, in seconds (s)
c: an unknown constant (machine and implementation), which cancels in the ratio
n: the input size
k: the exponent of n in the running time
2^k: k copies of 2 multiplied together
log_2(8): the base-2 logarithm of 8, which is 3 because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8
s: seconds
≈: approximately equal to
In words: doubling n multiplies the time by 8, which is 2 cubed, so the time grows like n cubed.
```

Quick reference: ratio 2 = linear, a bit over 2 = n log n, 4 = quadratic, 8 = cubic. This "doubling experiment" works for any polynomial-ish algorithm and is a good check against your analysis.

questions.prompt:
This function is documented as 'linear'. You time it at n = 50,000, 100,000 and 200,000 items and get 0.3 s, 1.2 s and 4.8 s. What is the most likely cause?

```python
def drain(items):
    out = []
    while items:
        # Front removal shifts items.
        out.append(items.pop(0))
    # Empty items; out keeps its order.
    return out
```

options.text: Python's `append` is O(n), so building `out` is quadratic
options.explanation: `append` is O(1) amortised. Building the output list is linear.

options.text: The timings are noise; a ratio of 4 is close enough to 2
options.explanation: A ratio of 4 measured consistently across two doublings is a clear signal of quadratic growth, not noise.

options.text: The garbage collector runs more often for larger lists, which is linear overhead
options.explanation: GC overhead doesn't explain a consistent 4x ratio. The algorithmic cost of pop(0) does.

options.text: `items.pop(0)` shifts all remaining elements each time, so the loop is Θ(n^2); use `collections.deque.popleft()` or iterate directly
options.explanation: Correct. Each pop(0) is O(len(items)), summing to about n × n / 2 shifts. The 4x ratio per doubling confirms quadratic behaviour. A deque's popleft is O(1).

questions.workedExample:
1. Ratios: 1.2 / 0.3 = 4 and 4.8 / 1.2 = 4. If time grows like n^k, doubling n multiplies it by 2^k, and 2^k = 4 gives k = 2: quadratic.
2. Find the hidden cost: `list.pop(0)` removes the first element and shifts the other `len - 1` pointers left.
3. Add up the shifts:

```formula
S = (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 0
S = n × (n − 1) / 2 ≈ n^2 / 2
S(200000) ≈ 2 × 10^10
where
S: the total number of pointer shifts done by all the pop(0) calls
n: the starting number of items
n^2: n squared, n × n
…: "and so on"
≈: approximately equal to
In words: each pop shifts everything still in the list, and those shifts add up to about half of n squared: twenty billion for 200,000 items.
```

4. Fixes:
   - `from collections import deque`, then `popleft()`: O(1) each.
   - Or don't destroy the input: `out = list(items)`, then `items.clear()` if needed.

The doubling experiment caught a bug that a quick read of the code ("one loop, so linear") missed.

questions.prompt: You need the **100 highest scores** from a stream of n = 10^9 records, on a machine that can't hold the whole dataset in memory. Which approach is best?

options.text: Load everything into a list and sort it: O(n log n)
options.explanation: The data doesn't fit in memory, and even if it did, sorting does far more work than needed: it orders all 10^9 records when you only need 100.

options.text: Quickselect for the 100th largest, then filter: O(n) average
options.explanation: Quickselect is linear on average, but it needs all the data in memory (it partitions in place) and has a Θ(n^2) worst case. It isn't a streaming algorithm.

options.text: Keep a min-heap of size 100 while streaming: O(n log 100) time, O(100) memory
options.explanation: Correct. Compare each new score with the minimum; only replacements need O(log 100) heap work. log2(100), the base-2 logarithm of 100, is about 7 tree levels, not an exact comparison count.

options.text: Compare each record against every record already seen
options.explanation: That is Θ(n^2), around 10^9 × 10^9 / 2 = 5 × 10^17 comparisons, and also needs all the data in memory.

questions.workedExample:
1. Constraints: n = 10^9, can't fit in memory, need only k = 100.
2. Heap approach:
   - Keep the best 100 seen so far in a min-heap.
   - New record bigger than the heap's minimum? Pop the minimum and push the new record: O(log k).
   - Otherwise skip it: O(1).
3. Compare the costs:

```formula
W_heap = O(n × log_2(k))
log_2(100) ≈ 6.6
W_sort ≈ n × log_2(n)
W_sort ≈ 10^9 × 29.9 ≈ 3 × 10^10
where
W_heap: the worst-case work of the heap scan, with memory O(k)
W_sort: the comparisons needed to sort everything
n: the number of records, 10^9
k: how many top scores to keep, 100
log_2: the base-2 logarithm: log_2(x) is the power you raise 2 to in order to get x
O: Big-O, at most a constant times
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the heap does at most about 7 levels of work per record and needs room for only 100 scores; sorting does about 30 per record and needs the whole dataset.
```

Most records are smaller than the current 100th best and are skipped after one comparison, so the heap scan is effectively a few passes' worth of work.

In Python, `heapq.nlargest(100, stream)` does exactly this. Thinking about which resources are scarce (here memory and a single pass) is as important as the Big-O of time.
